subject: 🦶 Trade Achilles' heel
body_html:
Plus: Fuel shock lingers | Friday, November 13, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Nov 13, 2026

Today, we look at the weak links of the global trade system — which helps explain this era of rolling supply disruptions and crises in which we seem to be living.

  • Plus, the latest inflation data suggests falling fuel prices are not translating into relief across America's supply chain. 😖

Situational awareness: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, appearing on CNBC this morning, pointed to the Commerce Department as the holdout in restricting Singaporean company Megaspeed from obtaining advanced chips.

  • It amounted to the behind-the-scenes tensions with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, first reported by our colleagues Maria Curi and Marc Caputo, spilling out into the open. More here.

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 865 words, a 3.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: The global economy's Achilles' heels
 

Illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios
 

A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system.

The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain.

  • That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around).
  • In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks.

By the numbers: They find that the share of global imports that face at least two of three major vulnerabilities has risen to 23% in 2024 from 15% in 2000.

  • The list of items with overlapping vulnerabilities includes basic materials like iron ore and more advanced items like lithium-ion batteries, smartphones and memory chips.

What they're saying: "It's not necessarily that trade has gotten less reliable," Tiago Devesa, a co-author of the report, tells Axios. "I think it's more that we have the realization that we actually want to understand what are the potential points of failure, so we can anticipate them."

  • "I think you could make a case that throughout all of these shocks, trade has continued to increase, and trade was actually a very important balancing mechanism," he adds.
  • "It's been increasing precisely in part because we've integrated the fabric of the global economy much more, and in particular, we've led a specialization effort that led to more concentration around the world," says Devesa, a senior fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute.

Reality check: Reducing vulnerabilities and building economic resilience isn't necessarily as simple as relocating a factory.

  • "Some companies just change their suppliers or factory from a geopolitically distant country to a geopolitically closer country, and they think that they achieved resilience," said Jeongmin Seong, a co-author and McKinsey partner.
  • "Even though you change the location of the final assembly, unless you eliminate the risk at this upstream level, you are still exposed."

Between the lines: The steady march of globalization paid major dividends in recent decades in making goods more affordable and powering global growth.

  • Now companies — and governments — are seeking to mitigate the vulnerabilities that system has created and that the last several years made plain to see.

2. Freight inflation warning
 
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

The latest producer price data suggests that the inflationary effects of the Iran war may be difficult to unwind.

  • Energy prices retreated last month — with diesel prices declining almost 8% — but the costs accumulated in recent months remained prominent across America's supply chain.

Why it matters: Higher fuel costs make it more expensive to transport key goods — including food — across the country, adding to the prices that businesses pay and possibly what consumers ultimately see on store shelves.

By the numbers: The Producer Price Index rose 0.3% in October, a sharp slowdown from September's 1.4% surge. Still, over the past year, PPI is up 6.5%, the largest 12-month increase in four years.

  • Producer food prices climbed 1.3% in October, with vegetable prices surging 27% (on top of a 31% increase in September).
  • Prices for basic organic chemicals — derived from petroleum and natural gas — jumped almost 4% in October alone, suggesting that elevated energy costs are still rippling through manufacturing.

Stunning stat: Truck transportation costs advanced 3.9% in October after a similar increase the prior month.

  • Prices are up almost 25% from a year earlier — the largest annual increase since May 2022. That puts the surge in transportation costs on par with the pandemic-era inflationary shock.
  • (A regulatory crackdown affecting immigrant truck drivers is also pushing up freight rates.)

What to watch: "Over the past year, what carriers charge to move and store consumer goods has risen nearly four times as fast as retailers' and wholesalers' markups, and those prices rose again in October despite easing energy costs," Richard de Chazal, an analyst at William Blair, wrote in a note.

  • "During the 2021-2022 freight spike, merchants raised markups to keep pace. This time they have absorbed much of the increase, leaving more to pass on to consumers if fuel stays high."
